solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (& 20dn.) Republican blind to truth, i.e. contender lie-spreading

indicators.note: the letters of the fodder are spread about and laid out afresh

explanation.surface: A swipe at a Republican candidate who refuses to accept the truth and spreads lies.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs on into 20 across. Fodder and indicator are fused in 'lie-spreading', which reads as one satirical compound.
explanation.definitionFit: An election denier is a Republican who refuses to accept a lost vote, blind to the truth of the count.

clue.text: Eye never starts to get litigious, follow?

indicators.note: starts asks for the opening letter of each of the two words before it

parts.note: the first letters of Eye and never
to sue is to go to law, the litigious course

explanation.surface: Private Eye, often threatened with libel actions, wonders whether lawsuits will follow.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to come afterwards as a result, which is a sense of follow.

clue.text: Once popped the question in the nude?

parts.note: to pose a question is to put it

explanation.surface: Someone who once proposed marriage without any clothes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popped the question' is the stock phrase for a marriage proposal, but here it just means asked a question: posed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in the nude is exposed, with nothing covered.

clue.text: What right-wing press would call Boris's sacking — yet Archer wobbles

definitions.text: What right-wing press would call Boris's sacking

indicators.note: the letters wobble out of their order

explanation.surface: Tory newspapers crying betrayal over Boris Johnson's fall, while Jeffrey Archer, the disgraced Tory novelist, wavers.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer is a Conservative peer and novelist jailed for perjury; he is only fodder here.
explanation.definitionFit: The pro-Johnson papers framed his removal by his own party as treachery.

clue.text: Surpass someone else's shag tally for a cost?

definitions.meaning: a jokey verb on the model of outrun and outdo: beat a rival at getting laid

explanation.surface: A boast about beating a rival's tally of sexual conquests, whatever it costs.
explanation.walkthrough: OUT-LAY: 'lay' is slang for a sexual partner or act, and 'shag' is British slang for sex. The question mark flags the invented verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the money you lay out on something is its cost.

clue.text: Mad Putin all but resolved to invade Switzerland's borders

indicators.note: to invade is to go into, so these letters are placed inside the others
the borders of a word are its first and last letters
resolved in the sense of broken up and worked out again, so the letters are reordered
all but means every letter except the last one

parts.note: taken as written, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A satirical jab at the Russian leader wanting to invade even neutral Switzerland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all but' drops the last letter of Putin to leave PUTI; 'resolved' rearranges that to TUPI, which 'to invade' puts between S and D, the borders of Switzerland's.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupid and mad both describe a foolish, senseless idea, so they are synonyms here.

clue.text: Date — score second time

parts.note: a try is a score in rugby

explanation.surface: Hoping to score on a second date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score second time' reads as a hope for the date's ending; the rugby sense of score is the one used.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the romantic sense: a secret meeting arranged between lovers.

clue.text: Old European kingdom puts pressure on aggressive power

explanation.surface: A historical kingdom leaning on a belligerent neighbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puts pressure on' reads as leaning on; here it is placement, P sitting on top of RUSSIA.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this north German state was a monarchy from 1701 until 1918.

clue.text: Wrecker Tory's about to be clad in fawn?

indicators.note: clad in means dressed in, so one set of letters is wrapped by the other

parts.note: a fawn is a young deer

indicators.note: about here means turned around and mixed, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of Tory's, taken as written

explanation.surface: A mocking image of a Conservative dressed up as a gentle young deer while doing damage.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a fawn is only a young example of the animal the wordplay needs.
explanation.definitionFit: A destroyer is one who wrecks or ruins things, so it is a synonym of wrecker.

clue.text: Presume maligned Diana was one

indicators.note: the letters are badly treated, knocked out of order

explanation.surface: A presumption that Princess Diana was badly treated by the press.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at Princess Diana, but the Diana meant is Diana Ross, lead singer of the Supremes.
explanation.definitionFit: A general-knowledge definition: Diana Ross sang lead in the Motown trio, so she was a member of it.

clue.text: Smart panties brandished

indicators.note: waved about, so the letters are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: Someone waving a pair of smart knickers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart panties' reads as fancy underwear; 'Smart' is the definition in its clever sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the Latin for wise; smart here is the clever sense, not the well-dressed one.

clue.text: Increase what you have and get stuffed

explanation.surface: Advice to grow your holdings, followed by a rude brush-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get stuffed' and 'up yours' are both British rude dismissals.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are coarse ways to tell someone to go away.

clue.text: Laid back presiding officer's seat

parts.note: the chair presides over a meeting

explanation.surface: A relaxed Speaker lounging in the official chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presiding officer's seat' reads as one phrase; the 's is 'is', so the chair is the person, and 'seat' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: an upholstered armchair is one kind of seat.

clue.text: Stunner, in fact a servant

indicators.note: the answer is in the letters that follow

explanation.surface: A beautiful woman who is in fact a servant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stunner' reads as a beautiful person; a Taser stuns with an electric shock.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the police weapon fires darts carrying an electric shock that stuns its target.

clue.text: Dick's short rule Mark overturned

indicators.note: overturned means turned over, so the combined letters are read backwards
short means abbreviated, so the word for rule is cut to its usual short form

parts.note: a rule is a regulation, often shortened to reg
the letters lost in shortening the word to its abbreviation
a dot is a small mark

explanation.surface: Someone called Dick briefly rules before Mark overturns him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts REGULATION to REG; add DOT for Mark, and 'overturned' reads REGDOT backwards. Todger is British slang for penis, and so is dick.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are vulgar slang for the penis, so they are synonyms in that sense.

clue.text: Everyone in Tunbridge Wells outskirts is onto Conservative lie

indicators.note: is onto signals that the following piece comes after, attached to what precedes it
in places one set of letters within the other
the outskirts of a phrase are its very first and very last letters

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Everyone in a Kent spa town, stereotypically true-blue, falls for a Conservative falsehood.
explanation.walkthrough: Tunbridge Wells is a Kent town famous for indignant conservative letter-writers, which makes the surface read naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall story is an exaggerated, unbelievable account, which is a kind of lie.

clue.text: Is my arse suitable for an agent of the state?

indicators.note: the letters are made suitable, fitted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether their backside is good enough for a state agent.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude surface question hides the fodder in plain sight: 'Is my arse' holds all eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a representative sent abroad on a government's behalf.

clue.text: Leader Lance — nut!

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a leader called Lance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lance' looks like a man's name and 'nut' like an insult; they are a weapon and a head.
explanation.definitionFit: The spearhead is the leading part of an attack, or the person leading it.

clue.text: Don't be so exploitative — it's futile

explanation.surface: A plea to stop exploiting people, dismissed as pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half splits the answer into two words, USE LESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Useless and futile both mean achieving nothing.

clue.text: Philatelist possibly changes first for one seeking to manipulate member

indicators.note: changes first means the opening letter of the word is replaced by another

parts.note: a stamp collector is an example of a hobbyist, so possibly flags a definition by example
the replacement opening letter, which the clue leaves the solver to find

explanation.surface: A stamp collector changes priorities and starts trying to influence politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue does not say which letter comes in; swapping the first letter of HOBBYIST for L gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A lobbyist tries to influence members of parliament or congress, so seeks to manipulate a member.

clue.text: Roll over Beethoven initially composed with Erich

indicators.note: initially picks out the first letter of the word
composed means put together, as music is, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A nod to the rock song Roll Over Beethoven, with a composer named Erich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll over Beethoven' is a Chuck Berry song title, so it reads as one phrase, but Roll alone is the definition and over is the cricket O.
explanation.definitionFit: A brioche is a soft sweet French bread roll, so it is an example of a roll.

clue.text: see 1dn.
E.J. Thribb's contributions are so contrary

definitions.meaning: Thribb is a poet, so his contributions take the form of poems

explanation.surface: A remark that a poet's pieces are perverse.
explanation.walkthrough: E.J. Thribb (17½) is Private Eye's fictional teenage poet, who writes obituary poems beginning 'So. Farewell then'. His work is IN VERSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the mathematical and logical sense of turned the opposite way.

clue.text: Rather opportune, Scotland's international body

indicators.note: loosely, only rather (partly) the letters are used

explanation.surface: A timely reference to Scotland's place on the world stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the comma, which a solver reading for sense skips over.
explanation.definitionFit: UNESCO is the United Nations' educational, scientific and cultural organisation.

clue.text: Clubs, etc for despised white-collar executives?

definitions.meaning: clubs, hearts, diamonds and spades: the four groups in a pack of cards
a sneering name for corporate managers, from their business clothes

explanation.surface: A golf club full of hated corporate bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' suggests golf or nightclubs where executives gather; it is the card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the card groups and the besuited managers are suits.

clue.text: Foreign head involved in crap move

indicators.note: involved in means wrapped up inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: crap and shit are vulgar synonyms

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A foreign leader gets caught up in some rubbish and wants out.
explanation.definitionFit: To shift something is to move it from one place to another, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Country finished if Republican gets in — this will get you over the rough

definitions.text: this will get you over the rough

indicators.note: gets in means enters, so this letter goes inside the others

parts.note: finished means over, as in the game is over

explanation.surface: A country is done for if a Republican takes power, a dig at US politics.
explanation.definitionFit: A Land Rover is a rugged off-road vehicle built to cross rough terrain.

clue.text: Old characters' energy overwhelmed by diarrhoea

parts.note: first part of RUNS; 'the runs' is slang for diarrhoea

explanation.surface: Some elderly people laid low by a stomach bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old characters' reads as old folk; the characters are letters of an ancient alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Runes are the letters of old Germanic alphabets.

clue.text: Bloomers inspire minors with dread, you might say

indicators.note: what you might say out loud, not how it is written

parts.note: awe = inspire with dread; kids = minors

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned knickers frightening children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' reads as baggy underwear; the flower sense is the definition. The sound match relies on a non-rhotic British accent.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchids are flowering plants, things that bloom.

clue.text: Inaugurate US president Don, steeped in evil?

definitions.note: the definition carries its object: to swear in a president is to inaugurate one

parts.note: first letter of SIN; sin = evil
to don is to put on, wear

explanation.surface: Donald Trump, sworn in as president, soaked in wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' is Donald Trump in the surface and the verb 'don' in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with its object: a president takes office by taking the oath before a judge.

clue.text: Secretary of State, yet dithering about check

indicators.note: the letters dither, shuffling out of place
they go round the other word

parts.note: first letter of YTE, the anagram of YET, split round the check

explanation.surface: A cabinet minister hesitating over a decision.
explanation.walkthrough: Yvette Cooper is a senior Labour cabinet minister; a first name as the answer is unusual, fair only because she is so well known.
explanation.definitionFit: Yvette Cooper has served as Home Secretary and Foreign Secretary, both Secretaries of State.

clue.text: You'll be glad to hear this goes down swimmingly

definitions.text: You'll be glad to hear this

indicators.note: the letters swim about into a new order

explanation.surface: Something welcome that is received very well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes down swimmingly' is British for being very well received, so the whole clue reads as one idiom; the fodder is hiding in it.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: welcome tidings are what a listener is glad to hear.
